title: Senior's toolkit: traits, reports and coverage
summary: Tag tests with traits and run slices of the suite, publish JUnit and TRX reports for CI, collect coverage with Microsoft's coverage extension or dotnet-coverage, and read what coverage does not tell you.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: slicing, reporting, measuring
steps.body: A suite of 3,000 tests needs slicing (fast tests on every push, slow ones nightly), reports CI can display, and a coverage number you know how to read.

toolkit.what: Tag a test, a class or (with an assembly attribute) everything, then filter on it.
flags: run everything else (the fast push build)
runs only when asked for (--explicit on), never by accident
skipped and reported, with the reason

toolkit.what: Write test reports for CI. JUnit XML is read by GitHub Actions and GitLab test reporters, TRX by Azure DevOps.
Line and branch coverage with Microsoft's coverage extension for MTP (package Microsoft.Testing.Extensions.CodeCoverage in the test project).
flags: collect coverage while the tests run
coverage, xml or cobertura (what most tools read)
include or exclude assemblies and files
toolkit.example:
dotnet add Shop.Tests package Microsoft.Testing.Extensions.CodeCoverage
dotnet test --coverage --coverage-output-format cobertura

toolkit.what: Turn Cobertura files into an HTML report with covered and missed lines (dotnet tool install -g dotnet-reportgenerator-globaltool).
flags: every report, from every test project
HTML plus a summary for a pull-request comment

toolkit.what: Microsoft's standalone coverage tool: wraps any command, so it also measures tests that start other processes (dotnet tool install -g dotnet-coverage).
flags: run the command and record coverage
toolkit.example: dotnet-coverage collect "dotnet test --solution Shop.slnx" -f cobertura -o coverage.cobertura.xml

steps.prompt: Match each need to the tool or option.
pairs: the push build must skip the 4-minute database tests
GitHub Actions should show failed tests in the run summary
a test that loads 2 GB of data must never run by accident
an HTML page of covered and missed lines
coverage for tests that start the app in another process

steps.title: What coverage does not tell you
body: Coverage counts the lines (and branches) that **ran** during the tests. It cannot tell whether any test **checked** what they did. This test gives `Shipping.Cost` 100% line coverage and catches nothing:
public void Cost_runs() => Shipping.Cost(80m);   // no assert at all

Use coverage the way seniors do: **low** coverage is a reliable warning (that code is not tested); **high** coverage proves nothing by itself. Look at the uncovered lines in the HTML report, and ask whether they are risky. A team-wide target like "80% or the build fails" mostly produces tests like the one above. Module 5 shows the honest measure: mutation testing.

steps.prompt: A pull request raises coverage from 62% to 91%. What should a reviewer check before being impressed?
options: Whether the new tests assert on results that matter, for example by checking that a planted bug makes them fail
Nothing: 91% is above the usual 80% target
Whether the tests were written before the code
Whether the coverage report is in Cobertura format
steps.explain: Coverage rises just as well with tests that assert nothing. Read a few of the new tests, or break the code on purpose and see whether they go red: that is mutation testing done by hand.

steps.prompt: Run the fast tests with coverage in Cobertura format, skipping the integration tests.
steps.explain: `--coverage` turns on the extension, `cobertura` is the format report tools read, and the trait filter uses the same name and value as the `[Trait]` attribute.
